mem.t: Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.

lessons.title: Self-Control Is the Spirit in Charge
lessons.theme: Self-control is not me holding myself in check, but letting the Holy Spirit govern me

v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Quietly ask: right now, what inside me most wants to take charge? Tiredness, a desire, an emotion, a thought? Acknowledge it without judging it, and then say, “Holy Spirit, please take charge of this place.”
teach: A car’s steering wheel can only be held by one person. Many people understand self-control as “gripping the wheel myself” — gritting their teeth and relying on willpower. But willpower is like a rubber band: the tighter you stretch it, the harder it snaps back. So people who try to control themselves by their own strength often swing back and forth between repression and indulgence.

Self-control is the last of the nine fruits. Paul does not say, “Control yourselves, and you won’t indulge your desires,” but “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” The key is “by the Spirit.” Those who belong to Christ have already crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts; now we are to “walk by the Spirit.”

So the secret of self-control is not to control ourselves harder but to hand over control more completely. A change of mindset: self-control is not “I keep myself in check” but “the Holy Spirit keeps me in check.” When the Spirit holds the wheel, we stop where we should stop and go where we should go.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Self-ruled people either indulge themselves or suppress themselves by their own effort — and both are the self on the throne. People living the self-emptied life let the Holy Spirit reign, and that is true freedom. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit lives in you and is willing to govern every part of you — how does that make you feel?
Who am I? — In which area do you often swing between “repression” and “indulgence”?
How shall I respond? — Which steering wheel will you hand over to the Holy Spirit today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was “led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” and after fasting forty days and nights, the devil told him to turn stones into bread. He had the power to do it, yet he chose not to, and resisted the temptation with the word of God. His self-control was not repression but a life wholly yielded to the Spirit, feeding on the Father’s word.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess that I often want to hold the wheel myself, and I end up either indulging myself or wearing myself out. Today I hand control over to you. Govern my body, my emotions, my desires and my time, so that I walk by you and bear the fruit of self-control. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a moment when you want to indulge today, pray silently: “Holy Spirit, please take charge.”
When you feel like losing your temper with one of “my 2,” stop and ask the Holy Spirit to take charge before you speak
lessons.noon: “Walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” — Lord, right now let the Holy Spirit take charge of me.

lessons.title: Paul Disciplines His Body
lessons.theme: For an incorruptible crown, we gladly train ourselves

v: I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.

lessons.still: Sit up straight with your feet on the floor, and become aware of your body. This body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my body is yours.” Then consider: whom is my body serving today — my desires, or my Lord?
teach: For the sake of a medal, athletes will rise early for years, control their diet and train every day. They don’t hate good food; they simply have a bigger goal. Paul says that those who compete “exercise self-control in all things,” only to receive “a corruptible crown” — in the ancient games, the victor’s crown was woven from leaves and withered within days.

Paul says, “I run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air.” A person with self-control has a sense of direction. He goes on, “I beat my body and bring it into submission.” My body does not lead me around; I lead my body. The word translated “beat” is a boxing term, describing a resolve not to give in to the flesh.

But this is not asceticism. Paul disciplined his body not to earn salvation but because he valued his witness to the gospel, lest he fail to live out what he preached to others. Self-control is training motivated by grace: because I am already loved, I am willing to live for the crown that cannot perish.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective — from the temporary to the eternal. Self-ruled people live for immediate gratification; people living the self-emptied life live for an eternal crown. Self-control is not losing enjoyment but gaining a greater glory — letting Jesus receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — God has prepared “an incorruptible crown” for you — what hope does that give you?
Who am I? — Is your life like “beating the air,” or does it have a clear direction?
How shall I respond? — In which bodily habit will you practise self-control today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed,” and often rose before dawn to pray. His body grew tired and hungry too, yet it always remained under the Father’s will. For the joy set before him, he laid down his own will in Gethsemane and walked to the cross.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for preparing an incorruptible crown for me. Help me not to run aimlessly but to live for you. I offer my body to you; Holy Spirit, help me to discipline it — not to earn your love, but because you already love me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose one bodily habit (sleep, eating, or your phone) and practise discipline in it for a whole week
Go to bed on time tonight, preparing your body for tomorrow morning’s devotions
Share your training goal with one of “my 2” and ask them to pray for you
lessons.noon: “I beat my body and bring it into submission.” — Lord, right now my body submits to your will.

lessons.title: Self-Control of the Tongue
lessons.theme: Whoever can bridle the tongue can bridle the whole body

v: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.

lessons.still: Close your mouth and be silent for a minute. Say nothing, and set aside even the talking inside your head. Then softly pray, “Set a watch, Lord, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.”
teach: One tiny match can burn down a whole forest. James says the tongue is like that: the smallest member of the body, yet it boasts great things and sets great fires. A cutting remark may be remembered for a lifetime; an unchecked piece of hearsay can destroy someone’s reputation.

James says, “Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also.” The tongue is like the bridle of the whole body; rein in the tongue and you rein in the whole person. The psalmist knew he could not control it himself, so he prayed, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” That is the secret of self-control — asking God to post a guard at the door of my mouth.

Self-control of the tongue includes: no lying, no judging, no gossip, no complaining, no hurtful jokes. In the internet age it also includes self-control of the fingers — the messages and comments we send. A change of mindset: before you speak, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it spoken in love?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Everything we do flows from the heart, and the words of our mouth come from the heart too. Self-ruled people use words to raise themselves up and push others down; people living the self-emptied life use words to build others up. Letting Jesus reign begins with letting him reign over my tongue.
q: Who is God? — God created all things by his word — how highly does he value our words?
Who am I? — Where do your words most often slip: complaining, judging, exaggerating, or gossip?
How shall I respond? — Which three questions will you use today to guard your mouth?
lessons.jesus: People marvelled at the gracious words that came from Jesus’ mouth. He spoke with authority, and he also knew when to be silent: faced with trick questions, he answered with wisdom; faced with false accusations, he said nothing. He also warned, “Every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.”
lessons.pray: Lord, set a watch before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. I confess that my tongue often runs out of control and I say many things I should not. Holy Spirit, govern my heart, so that everything that comes out of my mouth builds others up and carries grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Go a whole day without a single word of complaint
Before sending any message or comment, ask the three questions and only then press send
With one of “my 2,” replace one word of criticism with a word that builds up
lessons.noon: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” — Lord, right now guard my mouth.

lessons.title: Self-Control over Desires
lessons.theme: Grace teaches us to live soberly in this present age

v: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;

lessons.still: Honestly name one desire that has been tugging at you lately: eating, buying, watching, scrolling, being affirmed… Don’t be ashamed; lay it out before the Lord and say, “Lord, you are better than this.”
teach: In ancient times, a city without walls was open to enemies at any moment, and thieves could come and go as they pleased. Solomon said, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.” A person without self-control lets desires, emotions, advertising and trends come and go in their heart, until they are hollowed out.

What teaches us self-control? Paul’s answer is not the law but grace: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us… denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age.” To live “soberly” is self-control. Grace does not only forgive us; it also trains us.

Desire itself is not sin; God made us with hunger and longing. The problem comes when desire takes the throne and replaces God. A change of mindset: self-control does not overcome desire merely by “forbidding”; it overcomes by “a greater satisfaction” — when the heart is filled with Christ, secondary things return to their secondary place.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled people centre on satisfying themselves and end up enslaved by their desires; people living the self-emptied life centre on Christ and find true freedom. Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle — self-control is a lifestyle changed by grace.
q: Who is God? — Grace not only forgives you but also “instructs” you — how does that shape the way you see God’s grace?
Who am I? — Which wall of your heart’s city most needs repairing?
How shall I respond? — In which desire will you let Christ’s satisfaction take its place today?
lessons.jesus: The Samaritan woman had spent her whole life searching for satisfaction. At the well Jesus said to her, “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again.” He did not begin by rebuking her longing; he offered her something better. Only Christ can satisfy the deepest thirst of the human heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often let my desires sit on the throne. Thank you that your grace not only forgives me but also teaches me to live soberly in this present age. Fill my heart with yourself, so that I am satisfied in you and no longer led around by my desires. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose one desire and deliberately refrain from it once today, replacing it with prayer
Put off an impulse purchase for twenty-four hours before deciding
Take time you would normally spend scrolling on your phone and give it to one of “my 2” with your full attention
lessons.noon: “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.” — Lord, right now be the wall around the city of my heart.

lessons.title: Self-Control for My 2
lessons.theme: Gladly laying down my own rights to build others up

v: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are profitable. “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up.
Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.
Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.

lessons.still: Think of one of your 2. Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, which things that I am ‘allowed to do’ don’t actually build them up?” Wait for the Holy Spirit’s prompting, without rushing to defend yourself.
teach: A driver has the right to drive right up to the speed limit, but with an elderly passenger who gets carsick, someone who loves them will naturally slow down. This week we have seen that self-control is the Spirit in charge (Day 1), Paul disciplining his body (Day 2), self-control of the tongue (Day 3), and self-control over desires (Day 4). Today, self-control steps into our relationships.

Paul says, “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up.” Self-ruled people ask, “Do I have the right?” People living the self-emptied life ask, “Is this good for others?” “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” Self-control is not only for my own good; even more, it is for love of others.

Self-control for my 2 might mean voicing one less opinion, spending a little less time on my phone, insisting a little less on my own way. This brings our practice of the nine fruits to a close. Next week we enter “Forgiveness and Restoring Relationships” — the truest test of the nine fruits, in relationships that are broken.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The practice of 920 has reached the ninth fruit. Self-control is letting the Holy Spirit reign, and also putting others’ good ahead of my own rights. For Jesus, for others, not for myself — this is self-denial, and it is the way of life that builds what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — “Even Christ didn’t please himself” (Romans 15:3) — what does that show you about God?
Who am I? — Do you often defend yourself with “I have the right”?
How shall I respond? — For the good of one of your 2, which right will you lay down today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had the authority to ask the Father for more than twelve legions of angels, yet he chose not to; he had the right to be served, yet he chose to serve. He said, “The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve.” His greatest self-control was exercised for our good.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, for my sake you laid down your rights in heaven. Make me willing to lay down my own rights for my 2, not seeking my own good but the good of others. Holy Spirit, reign in my relationships, so that my self-control becomes an expression of love. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Let go of one “I have the right” insistence for one of “my 2”
When you are with your family today, leave your phone in another room
Tomorrow (Saturday), review with your spiritual companion: which of the nine fruits do you most need?
lessons.noon: “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” — Lord, right now I live for the good of others.
